teaser.en: Unusually for a palm, it branches, and its leaf strips are behind one of the best-known Digo plant names: *mlala*.

summary.en: *Mkoma*, the doum palm, is a tall fan palm that branches again and again, and its hard, shiny fruits are called *koma*. Its leaves, *mlala*, are the coast's great weaving material, and its fruit has saved lives in famine.

about.en:
*Mkoma* is one of very few palms that branch. Its trunk forks into two, and each branch may fork again, so an old tree can reach 25 metres with several crowns. Each crown carries stiff fan leaves on stalks edged with sharp spines.

The fruits hang in heavy clusters. They are hard, shiny and orange-brown, somewhat flattened, with a fibrous, sweetish pulp around a very hard kernel. The Digo call the fruit *koma*.

where.en: It grows in hot lowlands, along river courses and on the coastal plain: in coastal grassland, bushland and on sandy plains. On the drive inland from the south coast, its branched silhouettes stand out above the bush.

uses.en:
The leaves, called *mlala*, are the coast's great weaving material. They are split into strips and woven into mats, baskets, hats and other handicrafts, and used for roofing.

The fruit pulp and the kernel are eaten, and in hard times the fruit is an important famine food. The stem is tapped for palm wine. Trunks serve as poles and are hollowed into beehives.

culture.en: *Mlala*, the leaf and the weaving material, is one of the most widely known Digo plant names, as Pakia found. Mats and baskets of *mlala* have long been part of everyday life in Digo homes.

names.en: Pakia records the Digo name *mkoma*, also *mkoma lume*, and lists *mlala* among the weaving plants. The Mgombato dictionary gives *mkoma* for both the doum palm and the dwarf doum palm, and *mlala* as 'raffia', so speakers may use *mlala* for the leaf material more broadly. In Swahili it is *mkoma*, *mkoche* or *mlala*. In Giriama it is *mkoma* or *mlala*, and in Chonyi *mkoma*. In English it is the doum palm, and its scientific name is *Hyphaene compressa*.

reason.en: Same genus: the dwarf doum palm
The raffia palm, whose name overlaps with mlala in Mgombato
Also tapped for palm wine and used for thatch

definition.en: The leaves of a young fan palm (doum or borassus). The name depends on the palm's age because only young plants' leaves are useful.

use.en: Woven into mats, baskets, hats and other items.

meaning.en: From an older word meaning 'dwarf palm'. Mgombato glosses mlala as 'raffia', the weaving fibre.

shared_with: bangalala: the leaves of the mature palm

definition.en: The leaves of a mature fan palm (doum or borassus), which are not used for weaving.

shared_with: mlala: the leaves of the young palm

definition.en: The fruit of the doum palm.
A strip of raffia (mlala) about 5 mm wide.
Pieces of raffia (mlala) ready for weaving. The Swahili gloss, minyaa, refers to strips of doum palm leaf.
The hard edges of raffia (mlala) leaves, made into very fine thread for sewing plaits together into a mat or basket.
The tender, edible part between the stem and the leaves. Mgombato gives it for the coconut palm and for 'raffia' (mlala), which here is probably the doum palm.

mgombato: mkoma (mi) dwarf or doum palm (Hyphanae coriacea; H. compressa); mkoma, mlala, mkoche.
